familyProfiles/early/tagline: The undivided first centuries from which every later church claims descent.
familyProfiles/early/summary: The Christian movement from Pentecost to the great councils of the fourth and fifth centuries, before the lasting divisions of East and West. It produced the New Testament canon, the creeds, the episcopate and the patterns of worship that almost every later tradition looks back to.
familyProfiles/early/story:
Christianity began as a Jewish messianic movement in Jerusalem around AD 30, proclaiming that Jesus of Nazareth had been crucified, raised from the dead and exalted as Lord and Messiah. Within a generation the question of whether Gentile converts had to keep the Mosaic law was settled, at least in principle, at the meeting in Jerusalem described in Acts 15 (c. 49), and the letters of Paul show house churches across Syria, Asia Minor, Greece and Rome.

The faith spread along the trade routes and synagogue networks of the Roman Empire and beyond it: to Alexandria and North Africa, to Edessa and Mesopotamia, and by the third century to Armenia and, according to strong tradition, to south India. Sporadic and then empire-wide persecutions (under Decius in 250 and Diocletian from 303) produced martyrs whose memory shaped Christian identity, until Constantine's patronage and the Edict of Milan (313) made the church a public institution.

The early church was never uniform. It argued over the date of Easter, the readmission of those who had lapsed under persecution (the Novatianist and Donatist schisms), the authority of new prophecy (Montanism) and above all the nature of Christ and of God. The councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) defined the Trinity; Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) defined the person of Christ, and the last two councils left lasting separations with the Church of the East and the Oriental Orthodox.

No church today is 'the early church', but Catholics, Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and the Church of the East each claim unbroken continuity with it, and Protestants appeal to its Scriptures and creeds. Its leaders, the Fathers, remain shared authorities across the divides.

Its influence is hard to overstate: the canon of the New Testament, the Nicene Creed, the threefold ministry of bishops, presbyters and deacons, Sunday worship, baptism and the Eucharist, the church year, monasticism and the model of the council as a way of resolving disputes all come from these centuries.
familyProfiles/early/origin/event: Pentecost: the apostles begin to proclaim the risen Jesus in Jerusalem (Acts 2).
familyProfiles/early/coreDoctrines/0: Jesus is the Messiah and Lord, crucified and raised bodily from the dead.
familyProfiles/early/coreDoctrines/1: One God, confessed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit (defined at Nicaea 325 and Constantinople 381).
familyProfiles/early/coreDoctrines/2: Christ is fully divine and fully human (Ephesus 431, Chalcedon 451).
familyProfiles/early/coreDoctrines/3: Salvation through Christ received in faith, baptism and the life of the church.
familyProfiles/early/coreDoctrines/4: The Hebrew Scriptures and the apostolic writings as Scripture, with the 'rule of faith' as their interpretive key.
familyProfiles/early/coreDoctrines/5: The future resurrection of the dead and the return of Christ.
familyProfiles/early/focuses/1: Defining the boundaries of orthodoxy against rival teachings.
familyProfiles/early/focuses/2: Church order under bishops in apostolic succession.
familyProfiles/early/focuses/3: Catechesis and baptism of converts, usually at Easter.
familyProfiles/early/focuses/4: Care for the poor, widows and the sick as a mark of the community.
familyProfiles/early/strengths/0: Common inheritance of almost every Christian church.
familyProfiles/early/strengths/1: Remarkable growth without state support for nearly three centuries.
familyProfiles/early/strengths/2: Produced lasting theological syntheses (Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Augustine).
familyProfiles/early/strengths/3: Developed the conciliar method of settling disputes.
familyProfiles/early/criticisms/0: Increasing entanglement with imperial power after Constantine.
familyProfiles/early/criticisms/1: Hardening hostility towards Judaism in some writers.
familyProfiles/early/criticisms/2: Coercion of dissenters (e.g. the Donatists) once the church had state backing.
familyProfiles/early/criticisms/3: Its definitions of Christ's person left lasting schisms in the East.
familyProfiles/early/internalDivisions/0: Pope Victor I tried to excommunicate the churches of Asia that kept Easter on 14 Nisan.
familyProfiles/early/internalDivisions/1: Rigorists in Rome refused to readmit Christians who had lapsed under Decius.
familyProfiles/early/internalDivisions/2: North African church split over clergy who had handed over Scriptures in persecution.
familyProfiles/early/internalDivisions/3: Arius taught that the Son was a creature; the dispute ran for sixty years.
familyProfiles/early/internalDivisions/4: Council of Ephesus and the Church of the East
Condemnation of Nestorius widened the gap with the church in Persia.
familyProfiles/early/internalDivisions/5: Its 'two natures' definition was rejected by much of Egypt, Syria and Armenia.
